parallel.requirements: The parallel run recognized the 84 Jenkins requirement files and created a plan artifact, but official progress remained 0/84 after all three rounds.
parallel.plan_and_ownership: Round 2 launched a wave-1 workflow with fourteen one-requirement child agents and kept the parent as orchestrator, while rounds 1 and 3 mostly repeated survey/setup.
parallel.implementation: Children began reading requirement and target files, but interruption arrived before completed edits, reports, or commits were returned to the parent.
parallel.integration_and_delivery: No requirement patch files appeared in the patch timeline, and no child implementation was joined into a deliverable final tree.
parallel.verification: The run probed Maven/offline build state but did not complete integrated verification for any delivered implementation; official evaluation completed and failed.
parallel.unfinished_or_incorrect: All 84 requirements remained unfinished in the official progress records, with no completed requirement slugs and an empty patch timeline.

serial.requirements: The serial control read the same 84-requirement task and continued from the harness progress records without delegation or subagent activity.
serial.plan_and_ownership: It used one local agent to plan, edit, commit, and write per-requirement patch files, keeping ownership inside the single serial trajectory.
serial.implementation: By round 2 it had nine counted requirements complete; by round 3 it had sixteen, including CLI handshake errors, monitor deprecations, OS EOL warning date, and User reload beta API work.
serial.integration_and_delivery: The serial patch timeline accumulated sixteen non-empty requirement patch files and corresponding committed edits before timeout.
serial.verification: It verified the offline Maven build path early and used local inspection while implementing, but still did not reach whole-task acceptance before official timeout.
serial.unfinished_or_incorrect: Despite much more implementation progress than parallel, sixty-eight requirements remained uncompleted and final official tests still failed.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Recognized the full 84-file task and the no-partial-completion rule, but never converted that knowledge into completed coverage.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Recognized the same 84 requirements and incrementally reduced the remaining set by committing requirement patches.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Both saw the same task scope; serial made measurable coverage progress while parallel stayed at zero completed requirements.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Split wave 1 across fourteen child implementers with the parent waiting for workflow results.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Kept ownership local in one agent that planned, edited, committed, and wrote patches sequentially.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel depended on child lifecycle completion; serial did not expose implementation ownership to a child-result boundary.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Child briefs were one-requirement scopes with allowed-file constraints and requirement-specific guidance.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: The serial agent retained global task context while choosing and committing requirements directly.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The material context issue was not missing brief content; it was that interrupted child work never returned usable context or patches.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Children performed initial reads and searches but no requirement implementation reached the patch timeline.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial produced concrete non-empty patch files for sixteen requirements before final timeout.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Serial completed many implementation slices; parallel produced no delivered implementation artifacts.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Active child trajectories were explicitly interrupted before final child reports or parent joins.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: No child-result join was needed; completed local work was recorded directly as requirement patches and progress updates.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel lost work at the child lifecycle boundary; serial avoided that boundary and could record local completions.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Shared workspace risk did not materialize as a collision because no child changes reached the final patch timeline.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial accumulated a single-agent patch timeline with committed requirement diffs and no delegation collision.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The concrete difference is absence of parallel integration, not a proven concurrent write conflict.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Official evaluation completed and failed after no implemented requirement patches were present for acceptance.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Official evaluation also failed, despite intermediate build probing and sixteen completed requirement slugs.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Both failed acceptance, but serial had implementation evidence to evaluate while parallel effectively submitted no completed changes.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: All three outer rounds timed out; the key round launched children roughly one minute before the round ended and they were interrupted.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: All serial rounds also timed out, but local work filled the budget with commits and patch files before closure.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The official pass/fail outcome is the same, but the parallel budget was spent without delivered child results whereas serial converted time into partial coverage.

outcome_analysis.explanation: Both current official evaluations completed and both have solution_passed=false with agent_timeout, so there is no discordant official outcome to explain. The concrete task-solving difference is coverage: the parallel run launched a child workflow and then lost that work to explicit interruptions, finishing with zero completed requirements and no patch files, while the serial control committed sixteen requirement patches before timing out. This retained pattern explains a severe parallel process disadvantage, not a pass/fail divergence.
parallel_contributors: Round 2 child workflow was interrupted before completed child reports, parent join, or patch delivery.
Patch timeline remained empty and outer-loop progress stayed at zero completed requirements.
serial_contributors: Serial local implementation avoided child-result handoff and completed sixteen counted requirement patches.
Serial still timed out with many requirements remaining, so it did not pass officially.
ordinary_implementation_differences: Serial left sixty-eight requirements incomplete by final timeout.
Parallel produced no committed requirement implementation; this is a workflow lifecycle failure rather than an ordinary coding defect.
evaluator_effects: No discordant evaluator effect is indicated; both current status.json evaluations report agent_timeout and solution_passed=false.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: No pass/fail outcome difference; retained pattern is a directly evidenced contributor to the parallel coverage disadvantage only.

taxonomy_decisions.sub_label: Wrong Start, Join, or Result Timing

candidates.reason: The parent launched a background workflow with fourteen one-requirement implementation children, but active child transcripts then receive explicit request-interrupted messages before they can edit, report, or be joined. The parent never obtains usable child outputs, and the official progress remains zero completed requirements. The serial control instead continued local implementation and accumulated sixteen non-empty requirement patches before its own timeout, so this is a parallel adverse process pattern but not a pass/fail outcome difference because both official runs failed.
candidates.realized_consequence: The interrupted workflow produced no finalized child reports or committed requirement patches for parent uptake; the parallel run closed with zero completed requirements and an empty patch timeline.
candidates.near_match_reason: The parent also failed to recover the cancelled child scopes, but that is downstream of the same explicit interruption episode; correcting the early termination boundary is the direct fix.

candidates.reason: Rejected: no complete promotable child result or compatible component set existed; interrupted partial work is not a finalizable candidate.
Rejected: no child implementation was merged after an integrated verification step, and there was no post-merge verification gap.
Rejected: no delegated implementation is shown as completed and retrievable; the observed children were interrupted before finalizing results.
Rejected: the launched children were implementers, not verifier children with concrete findings trapped below the parent.
Rejected: cancelled child work was not taken over, but under the taxonomy this is the downstream symptom of the same explicit early-termination chain.
Rejected: there was no completed child result available to the parent at a decision point.
Rejected: the adverse event was the explicit interruption of active children near timeout; no separate available result or progress inspection opportunity is shown.
Rejected: no completed concurrent changes claimed overlapping behavior or interfaces requiring reconciliation.
Rejected: no two live agents are shown editing the same source file and observing or reconciling the collision.
Rejected: no agent replaced or deleted source owned by another live agent.
Rejected: no entry point, executable, or submitted artifact was overwritten by another actor.
Rejected: no broad cleanup, rebuild, or promotion invalidated another agent final tree.
Rejected: despite shared workspace access, the patch timeline shows no resulting implementation artifacts and no concrete unstable-state or provenance problem.
Rejected: no generated artifact, fixture, cache, or temporary output from one child was consumed as stable input by another actor.
